policy_title: Improve public transport, phase out fossil fuel vehicles, and reduce aviation
stated: Increase annual public subsidies for rail and bus travel to £10bn by the end of the next parliament, and invest an additional £19bn over five years to improve public transport, support electrification, and invest in new cycleways and footpaths, reallocating road building funds. This includes bringing the railways back into public ownership and investing in a modern, efficient, electrified railway with affordable fares, gradually bringing train companies back into public ownership as contracts expire. The policy aims to restore the fuel-duty escalator, oppose new road building, end sales of new petrol and diesel vehicles by 2027, end their use on the road by 2035, and introduce a £5bn per year vehicle scrappage scheme, supported by EV charging rollout. It will also introduce road-pricing. For aviation, a frequent-flyer levy will be introduced, domestic flights for journeys less than three hours by train will be banned, carbon tax will apply to aviation kerosene, airport capacity expansion will be halted, and skills for aviation workers will be invested in to transition to alternative jobs.

source.quote: Green MPs will push to: • Increase annual public subsidies for rail and bus travel to £10bn by the end of the next parliament to make public transport reliable, frequent, accessible and affordable, including free bus travel for under-18s. • Invest an additional £19bn over five years to improve public transport, support electrification and invest in new cycleways and footpaths; this includes the reallocation of funding earmarked for road building. Elected Greens will push for: • Investment in a modern, efficient, publicly owned railway, with affordable fares. • Greater investment in more rapid electrification so the rail network can be powered sustainably. • Bring the railways back into public ownership. • Train companies to be gradually brought back into public ownership, as existing contracts expire and rolling stock which is currently owned by leasing companies needs replacement. Green MPs will push to restore the fuel-duty escalator to this end and, as revenue declines, we favour the introduction of road-pricing, designed to ensure the protection of users’ privacy. Greens will oppose all new road building plans. Within a decade we want to see all petrol and diesel vehicles replaced by Electric Vehicles (EVs). We would push for an extensive vehicle scrappage scheme to support this rapid transition to EVs, with funding rising to £5bn per year by the end of the parliament, supported by the rapid rollout of EV charging points. Elected Greens would therefore also push for: • An end to sales of new petrol and diesel fuelled vehicles by 2027 and to the use of petrol and diesel vehicles on the road by 2035. Green MPs will campaign for: • A frequent-flyer levy to reduce the impact of the 15% of people who take 70% of flights. • A ban on domestic flights for a journey that would take less than three hours by train. • An end to the implicit subsidy for flying that results from kerosene being exempt from fuel duty: the carbon tax would apply to all kerosene for aviation sold in the UK • A halt to any expansion of airport capacity. • Investment in skills so that aviation and airport workers can move into rewarding alternative jobs as the number of flights declines.

consolidated_from: Increase public transport subsidies and investment
Bring railways into public ownership and invest in modernisation
Phase out petrol and diesel vehicles and introduce road pricing
Reduce reliance on aviation and halt airport expansion

bearing_set.reason: The policy's explicit core purpose is to cut transport emissions and improve air quality through vehicle electrification, aviation restrictions, and fossil-fuel phase-out — earning a direct verdict on emissions trajectory and air quality indicators.

Restoring the fuel-duty escalator, introducing road pricing, a frequent-flyer levy, a carbon tax on aviation kerosene, and forcing new-vehicle sales to EVs by 2027 all materially affect household transport costs; cheaper/subsidised rail and a £5bn scrappage scheme cut the other way — the net cost-of-living effect for different income groups is real and contested.

The domestic flight ban, carbon tax on aviation kerosene, and airport capacity freeze directly reduce aviation-sector demand and employment; the policy explicitly acknowledges this by funding skills transition for aviation workers — a concrete mechanism displacing job security and employment rates in aviation and fossil-fuel supply chains, with contested offset from green-transport job creation.

Vehicle-type bans (petrol/diesel mandates), domestic flight bans, and road pricing (which requires movement surveillance) each constitute non-trivial state coercion or surveillance, materially worsening freedom from mandates and privacy indicators.

Restoring the fuel-duty escalator, introducing road pricing, and imposing a frequent-flyer levy and aviation carbon tax are all new or increased taxes/levies that directly reduce the take-home income of motorists and aviation users.

Committing ~£10bn/year in rail/bus subsidies plus £19bn over five years in infrastructure investment plus £5bn/year scrappage scheme (~£15–16bn/year gross) creates a large fiscal commitment whose net position (offset by fuel duty, road pricing, and aviation taxes) is materially uncertain and non-negligible for debt-path sustainability.

Halting airport expansion, banning domestic flights, and applying aviation carbon taxes reduce UK business connectivity and international trade flows; conversely rail and public-transport investment improves domestic economic geography — the net effect on productivity and business investment is real and contested.

Fuel duty and road pricing are regressive (hitting lower-income, rural, car-dependent households hardest), while the frequent-flyer levy is progressive; the EV mandate timeline may be unaffordable for lower-income households despite the scrappage scheme — the distributional gap effects are non-negligible and move in conflicting directions across the package.

membership_note: This is a broad, multi-instrument transport and environmental policy covering taxes, mandates, prohibitions, public investment, and ownership changes — a bearing-set of seven is warranted by the distinct mechanisms identified for each fundamental, not by a generous reading.
